content: Terpenes are a diverse and extensive class of hydrocarbons primarily synthesized by a wide range of plants, particularly conifers. However, certain insects, such as swallowtail butterflies, also produce terpenes, which they release from a specialized gland called the osmeterium. These compounds are the primary constituents of plant resins and the turpentine derived from them. The term terpene originates from the word turpentine. When terpenes undergo chemical modifications, such as oxidation or rearrangement of their carbon skeleton, the resulting compounds are referred to as terpenoids. Some authors use the term terpene to encompass both terpenes and terpenoids. These compounds are the main components of essential oils found in many plants and flowers. Essential oils are widely utilized as natural flavoring agents in food, as fragrances in perfumery, and in traditional and alternative medicine practices, including aromatherapy. Synthetic derivatives of natural terpenes and terpenoids have significantly expanded the range of aromas used in perfumery and flavors in food additives. Vitamin A is an example of a terpene. Terpenes are biosynthetically derived from isoprene units, which have the molecular formula C5H8. The molecular formulas of terpenes are multiples of this unit, expressed as (C5H8)n, where n represents the number of linked isoprene units. This structural principle is known as the isoprene rule or C5 rule. Isoprene units can be linked in a head-to-tail manner to form linear chains or arranged to create ring structures. Isoprene itself does not directly participate in the biosynthetic process; instead, its activated forms, isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP) and dimethylallyl pyrophosphate (DMAPP), serve as the building blocks in the biosynthetic pathway. IPP is synthesized from acetyl-CoA through the intermediate mevalonic acid in the HMG-CoA reductase pathway. Alternatively, in certain bacterial groups and plant plastids, IPP is produced via the MEP (2-methyl-D-erythritol-4-phosphate) pathway, which begins with C5-sugars. In both pathways, IPP is isomerized to DMAPP by the enzyme isopentenyl pyrophosphate isomerase. As chains of isoprene units are assembled, the resulting terpenes are classified by size into hemiterpenes, monoterpenes, sesquiterpenes, diterpenes, sesterterpenes, triterpenes, and tetraterpenes. Types of Terpenes: Hemiterpenes consist of a single isoprene unit. Isoprene itself is the only hemiterpene, but oxygen-containing derivatives like prenol and isovaleric acid are classified as hemiterpenoids. Monoterpenes are composed of two isoprene units, with the molecular formula C10H16. Examples include geraniol, limonene, and terpineol. Sesquiterpenes contain three isoprene units and have the molecular formula C15H24. An example is farnesol. The prefix sesquimeans one and a half. Diterpenes are made up of four isoprene units, with the molecular formula C20H32. They are derived from geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate. Examples include cafestol, kahweol, cembrene, and taxadiene (a precursor to the anticancer drug taxol). Diterpenes also form the basis of biologically significant compounds such as retinol, retinal, and phytol. Sesterterpenes consist of five isoprene units (25 carbons) and are relatively rare compared to other terpene classes. Triterpenes are composed of six isoprene units, with the molecular formula C30H48. The linear triterpene squalene, a major component of shark liver oil, is formed through the reductive coupling of two molecules of farnesyl pyrophosphate. Squalene is then biosynthetically processed into lanosterol or cycloartenol, which are structural precursors to all steroids. Tetraterpenes contain eight isoprene units, with the molecular formula C40H56. Biologically important tetraterpenes include the acyclic lycopene, the monocyclic gamma-carotene, and the bicyclic alphaand beta-carotenes. Polyterpenes consist of long chains of numerous isoprene units. Natural rubber is an example of polyisoprene, characterized by cis double bonds. Some plants produce polyisoprene with trans double bonds, known as gutta-percha. Agricultural Applications: Research into terpenes has revealed that many of these compounds possess properties that make them ideal active ingredients in natural agricultural pesticides.
